title: Claude Code Has Been Leaking Secrets Through Its "Don't Ask Again" Feature
gist: Apiiro found that Claude Code's "Don't Ask Again" feature saves approved shell commands — including embedded credentials — into .claude/settings.local.json, leaking 1,122 secrets in that file plus 1,160 more in git history, shared settings and transcripts across 63 organizations. GitGuardian later found 31,088 secrets in such files on public GitHub (5,343 still valid), and generic scanners like gitleaks and TruffleHog missed many because they were embedded in shell commands.

insights.claim: When developers answer "Yes, and don't ask again" to a shell command in Claude Code, it saves the command as a permanent permission rule in .claude/settings.local.json, which can capture embedded credentials, passwords and API tokens.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: AI coding agents create new credential-exposure surfaces that existing secret hygiene practices do not cover.
insights.locator: The problem lies in how Claude Code handles command approval

insights.claim: Claude Code adds settings.local.json to the developer's global git ignore list rather than the repo's own .gitignore, so protection fails for folders that later become repos, clones on other machines, or files already committed — and researchers found Claude Code itself sometimes committed the file.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Machine-local ignore rules do not travel with the project, so leakage scales with team and machine count.
insights.quote: The rule never goes into the repo's own .gitignore, so nothing travels with the project to protect it.
insights.locator: When [Claude Code] creates the file inside a git repo

insights.claim: Apiiro researchers argue the settings.local.json file is itself a security gap because, to malware, it is a list of reachable systems and their passwords at the same path in every project.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Agent config files are a predictable target for infostealer malware — an opening for endpoint and secrets-security vendors.
insights.quote: it’s a list of the systems the developer can reach and the passwords that open them, one file search away

insights.claim: Apiiro identified 1,122 secrets in Claude Code .claude/settings.local.json files and another 1,160 in git history, committed shared settings.json files and agent chat transcripts in public repositories, affecting 63 organizations.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Quantified, multi-org exposure raises enterprise governance scrutiny of AI coding agents.

insights.claim: Exposed secrets from Claude Code settings files included cloud API keys, production passwords, access tokens and npm tokens.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: npm token leaks create software supply-chain risk beyond the affected organizations.
insights.locator: On some occasions, the researchers found

insights.claim: GitGuardian found 31,088 secrets in Claude Code's .claude/settings.local.json on public GitHub, 5,343 still valid at detection, plus 613 in Docker Hub images.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Thousands of live credentials indicate active, exploitable exposure — a demand driver for secret-scanning and rotation tooling.
insights.locator: Apiiro's findings were later reinforced by GitGuardian

insights.claim: GitGuardian had previously warned that Cursor, Claude Code and GitHub Copilot leave credentials scattered across config files, logs and shell history.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: The problem is category-wide across AI coding tools, not unique to one vendor.
insights.quote: Cursor, Claude Code, and GitHub Copilot leave credentials scattered across config files, logs, and shell history

insights.claim: Generic secret scanners such as gitleaks and TruffleHog failed to flag all secrets exposed via Claude Code, mostly because the secrets were embedded inside shell commands rather than in recognizable key formats.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Secret scanners tuned to key formats need new detection for agent artifacts — product gap for security vendors like Apiiro and GitGuardian.
insights.locator: Generic secret scanners such as gitleaks and TruffleHog

insights.claim: Apiiro warns the password-in-a-command pattern appears wherever an AI agent records what it ran — transcripts, memory files, handoff notes — and format-tuned scanners miss it in all of them.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Agent memory and transcript files are an expanding, unscanned attack surface.
insights.quote: a scanner tuned to key formats misses it in all of them

insights.claim: Apiiro recommends untracking .claude/settings.local.json with git rm --cached, adding it to the repo's .gitignore, rotating every credential it ever contained, deleting rules containing secrets, and referencing secrets via environment variables instead of typing them into commands.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Practical checklist for security teams auditing AI coding agent use.
insights.locator: At very very least, Apiiro recommends

insights.claim: Some developers are responding by keeping all AI files (settings, CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, memory) out of their projects and moving memory and docs to an MCP server instead.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Hints at demand for externalized agent memory/config services via MCP.
insights.locator: User MattV0 suggested an interesting approach

insights.claim: A Reddit user summed up reaction to the Claude Code leaks by observing that AI companies are said to be ignoring basic cyber security principles.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Reputational risk for AI coding tool vendors from security lapses.
insights.quote: Somewhere, someone said AI companies are ignoring basic cyber security principles
insights.locator: Commenting on the findings, Reddit user
